output.markdown:
# Product foundation

## Product
A software factory starter built on Cloudflare, for solo developers who want a sensible factory from the start instead of treating each project as bespoke work; the name is a working name ("software factory", or closer, "cf-saas-software-factory starter"), and the founder is not affiliated with Cloudflare.

## Problem
People vibe code, or cannot build their own software factory because the effort is ginormous. Today they invoke skills and plugins by hand and build their own environment. They use Matt Pocock's skills one by one, or similar tools one by one, including a set from a Y Combinator founder. They have nothing to build on top of, so each person becomes the bottleneck instead of a factory. Why leave single skills: an agency needs one shared setup.

## Persona
Solo developer. Alone, at a laptop, with a new idea. Wants a software factory to start from. What stops them: they have nothing to build on top of.

## Core scenario
A solo developer has an app idea and starts a SaaS, every time they have one. They need the latest and greatest tools and workflows. Today they search GitHub links and invoke each skill by hand. Done: they initialize their own factory and get to work.

## Also affected
Startup teams and agency leads, who also want a factory to start from. Teammates, on the developer experience side. Then users of the SaaS products built this way. See Open.

## Not for
Anyone not on Cloudflare.

## Feel
Simple, composable, succinct. Never complex, bloated or too much.

## Goals
1. By 27 February 2027: 50 GitHub stars.
2. By 27 February 2027: 5 outside repos using it, and 2 to 3 SaaS examples from our internal users.
3. By 27 November 2027: 1000 GitHub stars, and 3 examples of ours plus 5 from outsiders. Hope for traction, with people using it as a framework like shadcn, plugging in features.

Earns by: free and open source; the return is faster client work for us, meaning fewer bugs and more production-ready work instead of AI slop. Maybe a donation page; Buy Me a Coffee would be nice to have.

## Anti-goals
1. Custom skills and custom plugins. We ship workflows, not skills and plugins. We make nothing new; we build a factory for how existing skills and plugins work together. A skill bundled with a workflow is fine if it is useless outside that workflow.
2. Building on any host but Cloudflare. Cloudflare has the best developer experience: add services via wrangler and test locally with the same API. This keeps it a true software factory. Non-Cloudflare services such as Stripe are allowed; only other hosts are banned.
3. A hosted or paid version of the factory (a platform, dashboard or SaaS). Never. See Open.

## Assumptions
- People want a whole factory, not single skills. Not proven.
- Others share the problem. So far the evidence is the founder's own repeated pain.

## Open
- Product: the name is not fixed.
- Problem: the Y Combinator founder's skill set is unnamed; the founder forgot the name.
- Persona: developers, vibe coders, product and UI/UX people and new developers may use it as a starting point; whether they are users is not said. Problem names vibe coders as unable to build a factory themselves.
- Persona: the solo developer is primary, but the reason given to leave single skills is that an agency needs one shared setup; the two pull against each other.
- Also affected: what teammates and SaaS users should feel is not said; only the product's overall feel was given.
- Goals: 5 outside repos by February 2027 and 5 outsider examples by November 2027 are the same number nine months apart, and 2 to 3 examples of ours against 3 barely differ; one target may be too low.
- Goals: no number is set for donations, and "fewer bugs, more production ready" has no measure.
- Anti-goals: no reason is given for never building a hosted product.
- Assumptions: no test is set for whether people want a whole factory.

questions.question: Is the solo developer building their own SaaS ideas, client work for others, or both?
questions.why: Core scenario says an own idea each time, but the return is faster client work, so two readers picture different moments of use.

questions.question: Does 'anyone not on Cloudflare' include developers with no account yet who would deploy there to use this?
questions.why: Read literally it turns away people who would sign up, while the anti-goal only bans other hosts.

questions.question: What should the SaaS's end users and the developer's teammates feel, beyond simple, composable and succinct?
questions.why: Feel was given only for the product itself, yet Also affected names people who never touch the factory.

questions.question: How will you count outside repos using the factory, given you will never run a hosted service that sees them?
questions.why: Without a counting method the 5-repo goal cannot be checked on 27 February 2027, and the method (for example, searching GitHub for a file the CLI writes) may need a line in the product.
options: Search GitHub for a CLI file

questions.question: How many of your own client projects will start from the factory by 27 February 2027?
questions.why: Earning is faster client work, but no goal carries a number or date for it, so the one return you named cannot be checked.

questions.question: Is 50 stars by 27 February 2027 the real bar, given 1000 is due nine months later?
questions.why: A 20x jump in nine months means the first target either proves nothing or the second is out of reach, and one of them should move.

questions.question: Anti-goal 3 bans a hosted or paid version; does it also rule out paid add-ons such as premium features, support or consulting?
questions.why: A hosted product is a tempting build, but the Earns-by line leaves open whether paid support or extras count, so a paid-tier idea cannot yet be judged.

questions.question: Anti-goal 3 gives no reason for never hosting; what reason can a new hosted idea, such as a template gallery site, be judged against?
questions.why: Without a reason, a team cannot tell if a hosted gallery or registry conflicts, since the docs site already runs hosted.
options: We never run servers for users
It would end the free model
It would distract from the CLI

questions.question: Should the factory refuse team features such as multi-user permissions or shared agency config, given the solo developer is primary?
questions.why: Agency need is the stated reason to leave single skills, so team features are a tempting build the document neither bans nor defers.

questions.question: The reason to leave single skills is that an agency needs one shared setup, so what makes a solo developer, working alone, want a whole factory?
questions.why: The primary persona is solo, but the only stated reason to switch belongs to agencies, so either the reason or the persona in the document is wrong.
options: Set up once, reuse every idea
Real user is the agency lead

questions.question: At the moment a solo developer starts a new idea, what do they reach for today instead of single skills?
questions.why: The document names only skills as the alternative, but the strongest rival may be their own last project or a template, and the pitch must beat that one.
options: Start blank and prompt the AI

questions.question: What result by 27 February 2027 would tell you people do not want a whole factory and you should stop or change course?
questions.why: The key assumption is untested and the document has no point at which it counts as false, so the goals cannot separate failure from slow growth.
